title: How to write a business website project brief
seoTitle: Business Website Project Brief: A Practical Checklist
description: Prepare a website brief covering business goals, audience, pages, content, integrations and launch checks before requesting a development proposal.
sections: Start with the business decision

A website brief helps a development team understand the work before estimating it. Begin with the business problem: visitors cannot find the right service, staff cannot update content, or inquiries arrive without useful context. Describe what currently happens and what you want to improve. Choose a primary action such as requesting a quotation or discussing a project. Separate that action from business outcomes such as a signed contract, which also depend on pricing, suitability and follow-up. A clear brief gives both sides a way to judge the proposed scope.
Describe the audience and its questions

List the people who will use the website and the questions they need answered. A purchasing manager comparing software partners needs different information from a customer looking for opening hours. State which countries and languages you intend to serve. Explain whether your team can support inquiries in those languages. Identify the services you want to prioritise and any work you do not offer. Avoid creating a page for every possible location when the business cannot provide distinct, accurate information for each one.
Make a page and content inventory

Create a simple page list with its purpose, main action and content owner. For an existing website, record the current URL beside the proposed replacement so useful links can be preserved or redirected. Collect approved company details, service descriptions, original images and permission to use client material. Identify who will write and review missing content. If you need a blog, include who can draft, approve, publish and update articles. Content preparation is a separate piece of work; do not assume that adding a CMS will produce the copy for you.
Specify forms and integrations as workflows

For every form, explain what information is necessary, where a successful submission is saved and who checks it. Describe the confirmation a visitor should see and the message shown if submission fails. List systems that must connect, such as a CRM, appointment provider or existing business application. Confirm whether documented APIs and test accounts are available. Distinguish a working database submission from an email notification: those need separate checks. Do not place customer contact details or free-text form messages into analytics events.
Agree ownership, access and maintenance

Record who owns the domain, hosting, analytics property, code repository and uploaded media. Use company-controlled accounts and grant the development team the access it needs. Ask how backups are created and restored, how software updates are handled and what support is included after launch. If prices are quoted in euros or rupees, clarify the currency, taxes, third-party subscriptions and recurring charges. List your target date alongside the dependencies that can affect it, including content reviews and external provider access.
Turn launch requirements into acceptance checks

Define checks that someone can actually perform: open the main pages on a phone, navigate by keyboard, submit a labelled test inquiry, confirm it is saved and verify the success message. Check titles, visible headings, canonical URLs and redirects from replaced pages. Review performance using both laboratory tests and, when available, real visitor data. Analytics acceptance should include consent choices and receipt of the intended event, rather than the presence of a script alone. Search indexing and future leads are outcomes to monitor after launch, not guaranteed acceptance criteria.
Use the brief to compare proposals

Ask each provider to explain deliverables, exclusions, review rounds, responsibilities and what would change the estimate. Compare proposals against the same brief instead of comparing only their headline price. Keep unresolved questions visible and decide which features can wait. Bring the page inventory and workflow notes so the conversation can move towards a defined scope and a practical next step.

title: Website redesign SEO checklist: protect useful pages at launch
description: Plan a website redesign with URL mapping, redirects, crawl checks, sitemap updates and inquiry testing so useful pages and visitor journeys are preserved.
sections: Record what the existing website already does

Before replacing a website, export the important URLs and review the pages that receive visits, search clicks or inquiries. Keep a dated copy of this baseline. Include pages used in business listings, proposals and email signatures even when their search traffic is small. Identify which pages should stay, which need improvement and which are genuinely obsolete. A redesign is easier to evaluate when the team knows what it is trying to preserve. A visual refresh alone does not establish that search visibility or lead quality improved.
Map each useful old URL to its destination

Build a mapping table with the old URL, intended new URL and reason for the change. Preserve an existing URL when the page still serves the same purpose. When a useful page moves, redirect it to the closest relevant replacement. Do not redirect every missing page to the homepage; that creates an unclear journey and can hide genuine problems. If a page has no suitable replacement and is intentionally removed, return an appropriate missing or removed response. Separate historical unwanted URLs from current services that customers need.
Check search signals on the new pages

Give each important page a descriptive title, a visible main heading and content that explains the actual service. Confirm that public pages can be fetched and are not accidentally marked noindex. Review canonical URLs so they describe the intended public version. Keep administrative screens, private previews and internal tools out of search. Include public canonical URLs in the sitemap and link to them from relevant navigation or content. Structured data should describe visible, factual information rather than adding unsupported ratings, awards or results.
Test the launch before submitting anything to Google

Check response codes, redirect destinations and links using the final production domain. Verify both mobile and desktop layouts, including headings, navigation, images and forms. Submit a clearly labelled inquiry and confirm the server accepted it; do not count a button click as a completed lead. Test any email delivery separately. Check that rejecting optional analytics prevents tracking, then allow analytics and verify the expected events. Retain a deployment backup and a practical way to reverse a change if a critical journey fails.
Update discovery after the release

Submit or refresh the current sitemap in Search Console, then inspect the most important service and content URLs. Request indexing for eligible new or substantially changed pages when appropriate. Keep the old-to-new redirects available while Google and visitors discover the replacements. Search Console reports are delayed and may continue to show old URLs after the website has changed. A submitted sitemap or an indexing request does not guarantee inclusion or a specific ranking. Record submission dates so later checks can be compared with the actual release.
Monitor the right problems after launch

Review whether important pages remain accessible, whether Google selected the intended canonical and whether real inquiries still reach the team's workflow. Investigate unexpected server errors promptly. A large not-indexed total may contain duplicate, retired or unwanted URLs; the goal is to make the intended public pages discoverable, not to index every historical address. Compare search and inquiry data over a suitable period while accounting for seasonality, content changes and test traffic. Keep a short issue log with the affected URL, evidence and action taken.
Keep the migration checklist with the project

Make URL mapping, tracking verification and post-launch checks part of the website brief. Assign responsibility for redirect changes, content approval, inquiry checks and monitoring. Bring your current URL list and Search Console access to a project discussion so the scope can reflect the website's actual history. NekSoft can review the requirements for a business website redesign and the systems it needs to connect. The useful starting point is a clear inventory of what must keep working and what the new website should improve.
